questions.q: Ama walks 80 m east along a corridor, then 30 m west. Which statement is correct?
options: Her displacement is 110 m east and the distance she walked is 50 m.
Her displacement is 50 m east and the distance she walked is 110 m.
Her displacement and the distance she walked are both 50 m.
Her displacement and the distance she walked are both 110 m.
questions.exp: Displacement is the net change in position. Distance adds up the whole path, so it is never smaller than the size of the displacement.
questions.ref: Deck: Position and displacement in one dimension

questions.q: A trotro drives from Madina to Circle and straight back to Madina. For the whole trip, which statement is correct?
options: Its average velocity and average speed are both zero.
Its average speed is zero, but its average velocity is not zero.
Its average velocity and average speed are always equal.
Its average velocity is zero, but its average speed is not zero.
questions.exp: Average velocity uses displacement, which is zero for a round trip. Average speed uses total distance, which is not zero.
questions.ref: Deck: Average velocity and average speed

questions.q: Can the size of an object's displacement be larger than the distance it travelled?
options: Yes, when the object changes direction.
No. The distance travelled is always at least as large as the size of the displacement.
Yes, when the object moves at constant velocity.
Yes, when the displacement is negative.
questions.exp: The straight-line change in position can never be longer than the path actually followed.
questions.ref: Deck: Concept check: distance or displacement?

questions.q: On a number line, an object is at x = −3 m. What does this tell us?
options: The object is 3 m east of the origin.
The object is 3 m from the origin on the negative side.
The object has no position.
The object is moving backward.
questions.exp: The sign of x tells which side of the origin the object is on. It says nothing about how the object is moving.
questions.ref: Deck: Position and displacement in one dimension

questions.q: Kofi moves from x = +2 m to x = −4 m. His displacement is
options: positive, because the distance travelled is positive.
zero, because the positions have opposite signs.
positive, because x = +2 m is the larger number.
negative, because his final position is on the negative side of his starting position.
questions.exp: Displacement is final position minus initial position. Here it points towards negative x.
questions.ref: Deck: Position and displacement in one dimension

questions.q: A runner completes one lap of a track in 80 s. Which statement is correct?
options: The average velocity is zero, but the average speed is not zero.
Both are zero, because she returned to where she started.
The average speed is zero, but the average velocity is not zero.
Both are the same, because the time is the same.
questions.exp: She ends where she started, so the displacement and the average velocity are zero. She still covered a distance, so the average speed is not zero.
questions.ref: Deck: Average velocity and average speed

questions.q: What does a car speedometer show?
options: The average speed over the whole trip.
The velocity, including its direction.
The size of the instantaneous velocity, which is the speed.
The acceleration of the car.
questions.exp: The speedometer gives a magnitude at one instant. It gives no direction.
questions.ref: Deck: Instantaneous velocity

questions.q: A car travels around a bend at constant speed. Is its velocity constant?
options: No. Its direction changes, so its velocity changes.
Yes. Constant speed means constant velocity.
Yes. Velocity only changes when speed changes.
No. Its speed must be changing.
questions.exp: Velocity is a vector. A change in direction is a change in velocity even when the speed stays the same.
questions.ref: Deck: Acceleration along and across the path

questions.q: A car covers the first half of a journey at 30 km/h and the second half at 60 km/h. Compare its average speed for the whole journey with 45 km/h.
options: It is less than 45 km/h, because the car spends more time at the lower speed.
It is exactly 45 km/h, the mean of the two speeds.
It is more than 45 km/h, because 60 km/h is the larger speed.
It cannot be compared without knowing the distance.
questions.exp: Average speed is total distance divided by total time. The slow half takes longer, so it counts for more.
questions.ref: Deck: Average velocity and average speed

questions.q: Esi has velocity −5 m/s and Yaw has velocity +3 m/s along the same line. Who is moving faster?
options: Yaw, because +3 is greater than −5.
They move at the same speed, because the signs cancel.
Esi, because 5 m/s is the larger speed.
They cannot be compared, because the directions differ.
questions.exp: Speed is the size of the velocity. The sign only gives the direction along the line.
questions.ref: Deck: Notation: vector, magnitude and component

questions.q: The slope of the tangent to an x–t graph at one instant gives
options: the average velocity over the whole graph.
the displacement up to that instant.
the acceleration at that instant.
the instantaneous velocity at that instant.
questions.exp: Velocity is the rate of change of position, so it is the slope of the x–t graph.
questions.ref: Deck: Instantaneous velocity

questions.q: On an x–t graph, the average velocity between two times is the slope of
options: the tangent at the first time.
the tangent at the second time.
the straight line joining the two points on the graph.
the area under the graph between the two times.
questions.exp: Average velocity is displacement divided by the time interval. That is the slope of the chord between the two points.
questions.ref: Deck: From average to instantaneous velocity

questions.q: How is instantaneous velocity defined from average velocity?
options: As the average speed over the whole trip.
As the distance travelled divided by a long time.
As the average of the starting and ending speeds.
As the average velocity over a time interval that is made shorter and shorter.
questions.exp: Letting the interval shrink towards zero gives the velocity at a single instant.
questions.ref: Deck: From average to instantaneous velocity

questions.q: The x–t graph of an object is a straight sloping line. What is true of its velocity?
options: It is increasing.
It is constant, and equal to its average velocity.
It is decreasing.
It is zero.
questions.exp: A constant slope means a constant rate of change of position.
questions.ref: Deck: Concept check: reading an x–t graph

questions.q: A car's average velocity over an interval is zero. Must its instantaneous velocity be zero at every instant of that interval?
options: No. It can move away and come back, so the net displacement is zero.
Yes. Zero average velocity means no motion at all.
Yes. The instantaneous velocity is the average velocity.
No. Its acceleration must have been zero.
questions.exp: Average velocity depends only on the net displacement, not on what happened in between.
questions.ref: Deck: Concept check: velocity before any algebra

questions.q: An object has negative velocity and negative acceleration. What happens to its speed?
options: It increases, because the velocity and acceleration point the same way.
It decreases, because the acceleration is negative.
It stays constant.
It cannot be decided without numbers.
questions.exp: When velocity and acceleration have the same sign the object speeds up, whatever the sign.
questions.ref: Deck: Rule: speeding up or slowing down

questions.q: A car moving in the +x direction brakes. Which statement is correct?
options: Its acceleration is positive, because its velocity is positive.
Its acceleration is zero, because its velocity is positive.
Its acceleration is negative and its speed decreases.
Its velocity is negative, because it is slowing.
questions.exp: The acceleration points opposite to the velocity, so it is negative and the speed falls.
questions.ref: Deck: Rule: speeding up or slowing down

questions.q: "Negative acceleration always means the object is slowing down." This statement is
options: true, because negative means decreasing.
true, because acceleration is a vector.
false, because acceleration can never be negative.
false, because the object speeds up if its velocity is also negative.
questions.exp: Speeding up or slowing down depends on the signs of velocity and acceleration together.
questions.ref: Deck: Back to the poll: negative velocity and speeding up

questions.q: A ball thrown straight up is at the top of its path. What is its acceleration at that instant?
options: Zero, because the ball stops.
9.8 m/s² upward, because the ball was going up.
About 9.8 m/s² downward, the same as at every other instant.
Zero, because the velocity is zero.
questions.exp: Velocity is zero for an instant, but gravity still acts. The acceleration is the same throughout the flight.
questions.ref: Deck: Free fall

questions.q: Can an object have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration at the same instant?
options: Yes, for example a ball at the top of its path.
No. Zero velocity means zero acceleration.
No. Acceleration is the velocity divided by time.
Yes, but only if it is moving sideways.
questions.exp: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. The velocity can be zero at one instant and still be changing.
questions.ref: Deck: Instantaneous acceleration

questions.q: An object moves with constant velocity. Its acceleration is
options: constant and not zero.
zero.
equal to its velocity.
increasing with time.
questions.exp: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. If the velocity does not change, it is zero.
questions.ref: Deck: Average acceleration

questions.q: A cart moves to the right and its velocity changes from +6 m/s to −2 m/s. The direction of its acceleration is
options: to the right, because it started moving right.
to the right, because the final speed is smaller.
zero, because the speed is small.
to the left, because the velocity changed towards the negative direction.
questions.exp: The acceleration points in the direction of the change in velocity, here towards negative x.
questions.ref: Deck: Average acceleration

questions.q: A horizontal line on an x–t graph means the object is
options: at rest.
moving at constant non-zero velocity.
speeding up.
moving at its greatest speed.
questions.exp: The position does not change, so the velocity is zero.
questions.ref: Deck: Concept check: reading an x–t graph

questions.q: An x–t graph curves upward, with the slope getting steeper. The object is
options: moving at constant velocity.
speeding up in the positive direction.
slowing down.
at rest.
questions.exp: A steeper slope means the velocity is growing, so the acceleration is positive.
questions.ref: Deck: Reading motion graphs: slope and area

questions.q: An x–t graph is a straight line sloping downward. The object is
options: moving backward in time.
moving in the negative direction at constant speed.
at rest below the axis.
speeding up.
questions.exp: A negative slope is a negative velocity. The sign gives direction in space, not time.
questions.ref: Deck: Concept check: reading an x–t graph

questions.q: An x–t graph crosses the t axis (x = 0) at some time. At that time the object
options: is at the origin, and may or may not be at rest.
is at rest.
has zero acceleration.
has changed direction.
questions.exp: x = 0 means position at the origin. Velocity is given by the slope, not by the value of x.
questions.ref: Deck: Concept check: reading an x–t graph

questions.q: On one x–t graph, line A is steeper than line B. Which object has the greater speed?
options: B, because it stays lower on the graph.
They are equal, because both are straight lines.
A, because a steeper slope means a greater speed.
A, because it started earlier.
questions.exp: Speed is the size of the slope of the x–t graph.
questions.ref: Deck: Reading motion graphs: slope and area

questions.q: On a v–t graph, the slope gives the
options: acceleration.
displacement.
position.
distance travelled.
questions.exp: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
questions.ref: Deck: Reading motion graphs: slope and area

questions.q: On a v–t graph, the area between the graph and the time axis gives the
options: acceleration.
velocity.
displacement.
average speed.
questions.exp: Displacement is the integral of velocity over time.
questions.ref: Deck: Reading motion graphs: slope and area

questions.q: A v–t graph is a horizontal line above the time axis. The object has
options: constant acceleration and zero displacement.
zero acceleration and zero displacement.
zero acceleration and a displacement that grows steadily.
increasing acceleration.
questions.exp: A flat v–t graph has zero slope, so no acceleration. The area under it keeps growing.
questions.ref: Deck: Your turn: translate a v–t graph

questions.q: A v–t graph crosses the time axis from positive to negative. At the crossing the object
options: is back at its starting position.
has zero acceleration.
has stopped for good.
is momentarily at rest and then reverses direction.
questions.exp: v = 0 for an instant, and the sign change means the direction reverses. Position cannot be read from the velocity value.
questions.ref: Deck: Your turn: solution, slopes and areas

questions.q: A v–t graph has equal areas above and below the time axis. The object's
options: distance travelled is zero.
displacement is zero, but the distance travelled is not zero.
displacement and distance are both zero.
acceleration is zero.
questions.exp: Area below the axis counts as negative displacement, so the net displacement cancels. The distance still adds up.
questions.ref: Deck: Your turn: solution, slopes and areas

questions.q: A v–t graph is a straight line rising steadily from the origin. The acceleration is
options: constant and positive.
zero.
increasing with time.
constant and negative.
questions.exp: A straight line has a constant slope, which means constant acceleration.
questions.ref: Deck: Reading motion graphs: slope and area

questions.q: The constant-acceleration equations apply when
options: the object moves along any straight line.
the acceleration is constant during the motion.
the velocity is constant.
the object starts from rest.
questions.exp: These equations come from a constant acceleration. If it changes, they fail.
questions.ref: Deck: Constant acceleration: the equations and when to use them

questions.q: The acceleration of a particle increases steadily with time. Can we use v = v₀ + at?
options: Yes. It works for any acceleration.
No. The equation needs a constant acceleration, so we must integrate instead.
Yes, if we use the average speed.
No. The velocity cannot change.
questions.exp: Integrating a(t) over time gives the velocity when the acceleration varies.
questions.ref: Deck: Counter-example: the rule has a limit

questions.q: You know the initial velocity, the final velocity and the acceleration, and you want the displacement. The time is not given. Which equation is the best choice?
options: The one that links v², v₀², a and the displacement.
The one that needs the time t.
v = v₀ + at, because it is the simplest.
None. The problem cannot be solved.
questions.exp: Choose the equation that contains the unknown and the known quantities and leaves out the quantity you do not have.
questions.ref: Deck: Constant acceleration: the equations and when to use them

questions.q: A car brakes uniformly to a stop. If its initial speed is doubled, the braking distance becomes
options: half as large.
the same.
larger by more than a factor of two.
larger by exactly a factor of two.
questions.exp: Braking distance grows with the square of the initial speed, so doubling the speed more than doubles the distance.
questions.ref: Deck: Example 5: braking distance

questions.q: A car speeds up uniformly. Its average velocity over the interval is
options: equal to the final velocity.
halfway between the initial and final velocities.
equal to the initial velocity.
always zero.
questions.exp: For constant acceleration the velocity changes at a steady rate, so the average is the mean of the two ends.
questions.ref: Deck: Constant acceleration: the equations and when to use them

questions.q: Two stones, one heavy and one light, are dropped together from the same height. Ignoring air, which lands first?
options: They land together.
The heavy one.
The light one.
It depends on the shape of the stones.
questions.exp: In free fall every object has the same acceleration g, whatever its mass.
questions.ref: Deck: Free fall

questions.q: A ball is thrown upward. Ignoring air, its acceleration while going up is
options: smaller than while coming down.
the same as while coming down, downward.
upward, because the ball moves up.
zero at the top and downward elsewhere.
questions.exp: Only gravity acts, so the acceleration is g downward the whole time.
questions.ref: Deck: Free fall

questions.q: Which object is in free fall?
options: A coin tossed upward, after it leaves the hand.
A parachutist falling at constant speed.
A ball resting on a table.
A lift going down at constant speed.
questions.exp: Free fall means gravity is the only force. It does not depend on whether the object moves up or down.
questions.ref: Deck: Free fall

questions.q: A ball is thrown upward and returns to the launch height. Ignoring air, its speed on return is
options: greater than its launch speed.
smaller than its launch speed.
zero.
equal to its launch speed.
questions.exp: The motion is symmetric. The ball gains back the speed it lost on the way up.
questions.ref: Deck: Free fall

questions.q: A ball falls from rest. Compared with the first second, it falls in the second second
options: a larger distance, because it is moving faster.
the same distance.
a smaller distance.
no distance, because it has stopped accelerating.
questions.exp: Its speed keeps increasing, so it covers more distance in each equal interval.
questions.ref: Deck: Free fall

questions.q: One ball is dropped and another is fired horizontally from the same height at the same time. Ignoring air, which hits the ground first?
options: The dropped ball.
They hit together.
The ball fired horizontally.
It depends on the horizontal speed.
questions.exp: The vertical motion does not depend on the horizontal motion. The components are independent.
questions.ref: Deck: Independent components

questions.q: At the top of a projectile's path, ignoring air, which statement is correct?
options: The velocity is zero and the acceleration is zero.
The horizontal velocity is zero.
The vertical velocity is zero, the horizontal velocity is unchanged, and the acceleration is g downward.
The acceleration is zero, because the ball stops rising.
questions.exp: Gravity acts only vertically. The horizontal velocity stays constant throughout.
questions.ref: Deck: Projectile motion: the model

questions.q: What is the horizontal acceleration of a projectile, ignoring air?
options: g, downward.
g, in the direction of motion.
It depends on the launch angle.
Zero.
questions.exp: No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal velocity is constant.
questions.ref: Deck: Projectile motion: the model

questions.q: On level ground and with the same launch speed, which launch angle gives the greatest range?
questions.exp: Range is greatest at 45°. At 90° the ball goes straight up and has no range.
questions.ref: Deck: Projectile motion: the model

questions.q: On level ground and with the same launch speed, how do the ranges for launch angles of 30° and 60° compare?
options: The 30° range is greater.
The 60° range is greater.
They are equal.
They cannot be compared.
questions.exp: Two angles that add up to 90° give the same range, but the higher one stays in the air longer.
questions.ref: Deck: Projectile motion: the model

questions.q: A dart is aimed directly at a monkey and fired at the instant the monkey lets go and falls. Ignoring air, the dart
options: hits the monkey, because both fall the same distance below the line of sight.
passes above the monkey.
passes below the monkey.
misses, because the monkey moves.
questions.exp: Gravity pulls the dart and the monkey down by the same amount in the same time.
questions.ref: Deck: The monkey and the dart: solved

questions.q: In uniform circular motion, the acceleration points
options: along the velocity.
away from the centre.
nowhere, because it is zero.
towards the centre of the circle.
questions.exp: The velocity changes direction, and the change always points inward.
questions.ref: Deck: Uniform circular motion: the geometry

questions.q: An object moves in a circle at constant speed. Is its acceleration zero?
options: Yes. Its speed is constant.
Yes. Its position repeats.
No. Its velocity changes direction, so it accelerates.
No. Its speed must be changing.
questions.exp: Acceleration is the rate of change of the velocity vector, not only of the speed.
questions.ref: Deck: An opening question: acceleration at constant speed?

questions.q: At the same speed, a car goes around a tighter bend with a smaller radius. The size of its acceleration
options: decreases.
stays the same.
is zero.
increases.
questions.exp: The acceleration is v²/R. A smaller radius gives a larger acceleration.
questions.ref: Deck: Why the acceleration is v²/R

questions.q: A car goes around the same bend at a higher constant speed. The size of its acceleration
options: decreases.
stays the same.
increases.
is zero.
questions.exp: The acceleration is v²/R, so it grows with speed.
questions.ref: Deck: Why the acceleration is v²/R

questions.q: The time taken for one complete circle is called the
options: frequency.
angular speed.
displacement.
period.
questions.exp: The period T is the time for one revolution. The frequency f is its inverse.
questions.ref: Deck: Period, frequency and angular speed

questions.q: A train moves east. A passenger walks towards the front of the train. Relative to the ground, the passenger's speed is
options: less than the train's speed.
equal to the train's speed.
greater than the train's speed.
zero.
questions.exp: Relative velocities add as vectors. Walking forward adds to the train's velocity.
questions.ref: Deck: Relative velocity: notation, rule and the train

questions.q: The same passenger walks towards the back of the train. Relative to the ground, the passenger's speed is
options: greater than the train's speed.
less than the train's speed.
equal to the train's speed.
the same as the walking speed.
questions.exp: Walking backward subtracts from the velocity of the train.
questions.ref: Deck: Relative velocity: notation, rule and the train

questions.q: A boat points straight across a river with a current. Relative to the ground, the boat
options: goes straight across.
drifts upstream.
stops moving.
drifts downstream while crossing.
questions.exp: The velocity of the boat relative to the ground is the sum of its velocity relative to the water and the velocity of the water.
questions.ref: Deck: Example 7: crossing a river

questions.q: To travel straight across a river with a current, the boat must be pointed
options: straight across.
somewhat downstream.
somewhat upstream.
along the bank.
questions.exp: The upstream part of the boat's velocity cancels the current.
questions.ref: Deck: Example 7: crossing a river

questions.q: A boat points straight across a river at a fixed speed relative to the water. A stronger current makes the crossing time
options: shorter.
longer.
zero.
unchanged, because the current has no component across the river.
questions.exp: Only the velocity component across the river decides how long the crossing takes.
questions.ref: Deck: Example 7: crossing a river
